metadata.title: Does money buy strong performance in PISA? (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD PISA in Focus brief synthesizes results from PISA 2009 (reading, mathematics and science) and PISA 2009 school-success analyses, rather than presenting a new student-level statistical model. The brief discusses relationships between country-level indicators (e.g., per-capita GDP, cumulative education expenditure per student) and PISA mean reading performance, which are typically derived from PISA’s complex sampling design and scaling procedures. Because the document does not report an analytic micro-dataset, weight variables, or replicate-weight procedures, it is not possible to confirm whether student/sampling weights (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) were applied in a re-analysis. For replication with PISA microdata, analysts should use the official PISA sampling weights and replicate weights provided in the international database when estimating country means and uncertainty.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The document is a policy brief that reports descriptive/associational findings at the country level (e.g., thresholds in per-capita GDP and education expenditure versus mean PISA reading performance) and does not provide an explicit student-level predictive model with documented plausible-value (PV) or missing-data handling. PVs are generated for cognitive achievement scales in PISA, but this brief does not specify whether it uses PV-based estimates, WLE/theta, or already-published country means. Missing-data handling is therefore not reported because no new microdata estimation procedure is described.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The brief does not define an analytic microdata subsample. It reports country-level relationships using PISA 2009 results (notably mean reading performance) and country-level education and economic indicators, and it notes that some jurisdictions did not report per-capita GDP data (Albania, Dubai (UAE), Liechtenstein, Qatar) and that 23 partner countries/economies did not report cumulative education expenditure data.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD PISA in Focus brief synthesizes PISA 2009 evidence to argue that national wealth and total education spending are not sufficient to explain differences in student performance. It reports threshold-like patterns: for per-capita GDP up to around USD 20,000, higher wealth is associated with higher mean reading scores, but above that level wealth is no longer a predictor. Similarly, cumulative education expenditure per student shows little relationship with performance after roughly USD 35,000 per student, with high-spending systems (e.g., Luxembourg, Norway, Switzerland, United States) performing similarly to lower-spending ones. The brief then highlights more actionable correlates in high-income economies: prioritizing teacher quality (e.g., teacher salaries and professional status) over smaller class sizes, and adopting inclusive systems with high expectations for all students (retaining/transfer/grouping practices linked to higher mean reading performance). Because the document does not provide a new ML model, PV handling, or missing-data procedures, the results should be interpreted as descriptive/associational policy messages rather than causal estimates.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a policy brief that summarizes published PISA 2009 findings rather than presenting an original empirical ML analysis with an explicit student-level dataset, model specification, PV handling, missing-data strategy, or reported sample sizes. Consequently, fields such as total_students, per-country n_students, and ML techniques are not available from the provided text, and the extraction focuses on the reported country-level relationships and policy implications.
